title: Create With AI, Ethically
goal: Your kid makes something real with AI, like a website, a story or a poster, and stays the one in charge. They decide what it's for and who it's for, do the parts that need them, let AI help with the rest, steer it until it matches what they had in mind, and are honest about what AI made.
need: A grown-up's account on an AI tool
A real project with a real person waiting for it, like a party invitation, a poster for a sale or a recipe card for a grandparent
A notebook for the plan and the who-did-what list

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Banning AI from creative work and letting it do everything fail the same way. Help them decide which parts are theirs, keep them the boss of the result, and make saying 'AI helped' normal.

plan.what: Decide what's theirs and plan the project (Steps 1 and 2).
Make it, then test it on the person it's for (Steps 3 and 4).

troubleshoot.q: They want AI to do all of it
troubleshoot.a: Ask what they'd be proud of. Then make sure that part, the idea, the choices or the final words, stays theirs.
It isn't, if they're honest about it and the decisions are theirs. Your family rules still decide where AI isn't allowed, like anything meant to be in their own words.

troubleshoot.q: They want to copy someone else's work or style
troubleshoot.a: Use AI to make something new, not a copy of a real artist's work. That style took the artist years; your kid's own idea is what makes it theirs.

lesson.text: AI can make a lot, fast. What makes a project yours is the parts only you can do: knowing who it's for, deciding what it should be, steering it until it's right, and being honest about what AI made.
lesson.before: 'The AI made it, so it's not really mine.'

model.line: Gathers what the client needs and wants.
AI makes a mockup from his ideas, and does the coding.
He prompts changes until it's the way he wants it.
He writes the email to the client himself. No secret about the AI.

lesson.modelNote: The coding is all done by AI. The client, the ideas, the decisions and the final word are his. That's what makes it his work.

steps.title: Decide what's yours
steps.why: Before AI touches anything, decide which parts you'll do yourself. Those are what make it yours.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a real project and splits it up, using the Who does what card: what they'll do, what AI could help with, and what AI should never do for them.
steps.you: Ask: 'What part would you be proud of?' Help them keep that part for themselves.
ask: Which part should only you do?
steps.tip: Real audiences make the best projects: a client, a grandparent, a friend's birthday.

levels.explore: Pick a project, and say one part you'll do yourself.
levels.develop: Fill in the Who does what card for your project.
levels.extend: Pick one part AI could do well, keep it for yourself anyway, and explain what you'd lose by handing it over.

steps.title: Plan it like a pro
steps.why: The best results start with a clear brief: who it's for, what they need, and what it should feel like.
steps.kid: Your kid writes a short brief, using the Brief card: who it's for, what they need, what it should look and feel like, and what to avoid.
steps.you: Play the client or the audience. Answer their questions like a real customer would.
ask: What does the person you're making this for need?
What would make them say wow?
steps.tip: Gather the real information first. AI is only as good as what you give it.

levels.explore: Say who it's for and what they'd like.
levels.develop: Write a full brief with every part of the card.
levels.extend: Interview the real person it's for, and build the brief from their answers.

steps.title: Make it with AI
steps.why: AI is great at first drafts, code and options. Your kid gives it the brief and their own ideas.
steps.kid: Your kid gives AI the brief and asks for a first version, using the Ask AI for card: a mockup, a draft, options, or the parts they decided AI could do.
steps.you: Stay close. Use a made-up name for the client in the prompt, and add the real one yourself at the end.
ask: What's missing that only you know?
steps.tip: Ask for two or three options. Choosing between them is where their taste shows.

levels.explore: Ask AI for one idea, and say what you like and don't like.
levels.develop: Get a first version from your brief, and list three things to change.
levels.extend: Ask for three different options, and explain which fits the brief best.

steps.title: Test it on the person it's for
steps.why: The first version is AI's. The final version should be theirs.
steps.kid: Your kid shows the unfinished version to the person it's for, notes what they say and where they get confused, then uses the Steer it card to change it and does any part they decided was theirs.
steps.you: Ask 'Is this what you wanted?' before 'Is it finished?' They decide when it's done.
ask: Is it the way you want it yet?
What did you change that AI didn't think of?
steps.tip: If AI keeps doing too much, stop and do that part yourself. That's steering too.

levels.explore: Ask for one change, and say if it's better.
levels.develop: Steer it until it matches your brief, and do your own part.
levels.extend: Watch the person use it without explaining anything, write down every place they hesitate, and fix those first.

steps.title: Share it, honestly
steps.why: Being honest about AI is part of doing it right. It builds trust with the people you make things for.
steps.kid: Your kid shares the project with the person it's for and says how it was made, using the Credit it card: what they did, what AI did, and what they decided.
steps.you: Show them it's normal to say AI helped. Hiding it is what makes it feel like cheating.
ask: What will you say about how you made it?
steps.tip: A simple line works: 'I designed it and made the decisions, and AI helped with the code.'

levels.explore: Show it to someone, and say one part you did and one part AI did.
levels.develop: Share it with the person it's for, with an honest how-I-made-it line.
levels.extend: Before you share, find the AI rules of the place it's going, like a contest, a market listing or a video site, and follow them.

conclusion.headline: They make things with AI, and they stay in charge.
conclusion.text: Look at what they make next. The idea, the choices and the last word should still be theirs, and they'll say so without being asked.
conclusion.celebrate: When they finish a project with AI help, say: 'You made every decision, and you told the truth about how. It's yours.'
extensions: Make the same small project with and without AI, and compare

signs: They decide what's theirs before opening the AI tool
They keep steering until it matches what they wanted
They say openly when AI helped
makeItReal: This week, whenever anyone in the family shares something AI helped make, you included, add one honest line: 'AI helped with...'

fromHome.text: My son has a small web design business. He gathers what his clients want, gives his ideas to Claude for a mockup and the coding, then prompts changes until it's the way he wants it. He writes the email to the client himself, and he doesn't hide that AI did the coding.

photo.caption: At his desk, steering the mockup.

classroom.intro: Making something real for a real person works well in class when each group has a client inside the school. Groups plan and do their own parts on paper, and you run the AI requests on the projector.

tips.d: Pick projects people in the building actually need: a poster for the book fair, an invitation for a class event, a sign for the school garden. The office or another teacher can be the client.
AI tools have age limits, so you run them from your account on the projector, following school policy. Groups hand you their written brief and use made-up names, never real student details.
Give each group a brief writer, a designer who does the hand-made parts, a steerer who decides what to change, and a credit keeper who fills in the Credit it card as they go.
For Step 4, the client visits the class or groups take the draft to them with you. Groups watch the client react, note where they get confused, and steer from there.
Explore students pick one part they'll do themselves, Develop students fill in the full Who does what card, and Extend students keep a part AI could do well and explain what they'd lose.
End with a gallery walk where each project shows its how-it-was-made line from the Credit it card. Talk as a class about why saying 'AI helped' is normal and keeps it fair.

classroom.timing: Plan three or four sessions of 40 to 45 minutes: Steps 1 and 2 on paper, Step 3 on the projector, Step 4 with the client, then Step 5 as a gallery walk. Hand-made parts can be finished at home.
